questions.text:
A survey found that 45% of Year 12 students at a school participate in a drama club, and 30% do community service. 10% of students do both.

(i) Draw a two-way table to display this information.
(ii) Find the probability that a randomly selected Year 12 student participates in a drama club but does NOT do community service.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correctly sets up two-way table with Drama/No Drama vs Community Service/No Community Service. P(Drama only) = 0.45 - 0.10 = 0.35. Table values: Both = 0.10, Drama only = 0.35, Community Service only = 0.20, Neither = 0.35. Merit: All values correct with clear working shown.

questions.text: Using the information from Question 1a, determine whether participating in a drama club and playing a community service are independent events. You must justify your answer with appropriate calculations.
questions.markingGuide: Merit: For independence, P(Drama AND Sport) should equal P(Drama) × P(Sport). P(Drama) × P(Sport) = 0.45 × 0.30 = 0.135. P(Drama AND Sport) = 0.10. Since 0.10 ≠ 0.135, the events are NOT independent. Excellence: Clear logical reasoning with correct calculations, concluding that participation in drama clubs and community services are not independent — students in drama clubs are slightly less likely to also play a community service than would be expected if they were independent.

questions.text:
A school health screening tests students for iron deficiency. The test has the following properties:
• 5% of students have iron deficiency.
• If a student has iron deficiency, the test gives a positive result 90% of the time.
• If a student does not have iron deficiency, the test gives a positive result 8% of the time (false positive).

Draw a probability tree diagram to represent this situation. Use a population of 5,000 students to help with your calculations.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct tree with branches: Iron Deficiency (0.05) / No Deficiency (0.95), then Test+ / Test- for each. Using 5,000: Iron Def = 250, No Def = 4,750. Iron Def & Test+ = 225, Iron Def & Test- = 25, No Def & Test+ = 380, No Def & Test- = 4,370.

questions.text:
Using your tree diagram from Question 2a, calculate:
(i) The probability that a randomly selected student tests positive.
(ii) The probability that a student actually has iron deficiency, given that they tested positive.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: P(Test+) = (225 + 380)/5000 = 605/5000 = 0.121. Merit: P(Iron Def | Test+) = 225/605 = 0.372 (approximately 37.2%). Working must show conditional probability calculation clearly. Common error: confusing P(Test+ | Iron Def) with P(Iron Def | Test+).

questions.text: Discuss what the answer to Question 2b(ii) means for a student who receives a positive test result. Explain why the result might be surprising and what implications this has for school health screening programmes.
questions.markingGuide: Excellence: Despite the test being 90% accurate, a positive result only means about a 37% chance of actually having iron deficiency. This is surprising because most people assume a 90% accurate test means a 90% chance of having the condition if you test positive. The low base rate (5%) means that the number of false positives from the large healthy population overwhelms the true positives. Implications: a single positive test should not be used for definitive diagnosis — follow-up blood work is needed. This demonstrates the base rate fallacy and why screening programmes must be carefully designed and communicated.

questions.text:
A study investigated whether taking regular short breaks during study improves test performance. The results are shown in the table below.

Calculate the risk of scoring above 70% for each group.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Risk for break group = 48/150 = 0.32 (32.0%). Risk for no-break group = 32/150 = 0.213 (21.3%).

questions.text: Calculate the relative risk of scoring above 70% for those who took regular breaks compared to those who did not. Interpret this value in context.
questions.markingGuide: Merit: Relative risk = 0.32/0.213 = 1.50. Interpretation: Students who took regular breaks were 1.50 times as likely to score above 70% as those who did not, meaning they had about 50% more chance of achieving a high score. Must include both the calculation and a correct contextual interpretation.
